"Shimazaki, I've decided to dedicate this summer to Seibu."

On July 31st, the last day of the first semester, Naruse blurted out something weird again on our way home. Naruse is always weird. I should know; I've had a front-row seat for most of the fourteen-year history of Akari Naruse.

I'm Miyuki Shimazaki, an ordinary person who happened to be born in the same apartment building as Naruse. Ever since we were at the private Akebi Kindergarten, Naruse stood out from the other kids. She ran faster than anyone, was great at drawing and singing, and could write hiragana and katakana perfectly. Everyone raved about how amazing "Akari-chan" was. She, however, took it all in stride, remaining completely unfazed and never letting it go to her head. I used to be proud just to live in the same building as her.

But as the years went by, Naruse became increasingly isolated. Because she could do everything on her own, she didn't seem to need anyone else. Even though she wasn't doing it on purpose, people around her interpreted it as her being stuck-up.
By the time we hit fifth grade, Naruse was being explicitly ignored by the other girls. Even though we were in the same class, I didn't step in to protect her, prioritizing my own social survival.

One day, I ran into Naruse in the apartment entrance, and she was carrying a large load. Thinking it would be rude to ignore her, I asked, "Where are you going?" She just said, "Shimazaki, I've decided to master the art of soap bubbles," and headed out.

A few days later, Naruse appeared on "Gururin Wide," a local evening news program. There she was, the "Soap Bubble Prodigy," creating bubbles as big as a wealthy person's dog and explaining to the local comedian acting as a reporter that "the ratio of glue is crucial."
The next day, a group of girls surrounded Naruse at school. After class, a soap bubble workshop was held, led by Naruse herself.

Now that we're in eighth grade, Naruse continues to live life at her own pace, completely unconcerned with what others think. We're in different classes now, so I don't know exactly what her daily life is like, but there doesn't seem to be any major bullying. I hear she just spends her time running her heart out in the track and field club.
Under the pretext of living in the same apartment building, I walk to and from school with her.
"What do you mean, dedicate your summer to Seibu?"
"I'm going to go to Seibu every day."

I knew what Naruse was getting at. The Seibu Otsu department store, the only one in our city of Otsu, was set to close its doors in a month, on August 31st. Apparently, the building was going to be torn down and replaced with apartments. With forty-four years of history coming to an end, the local residents were heartbroken.

I'd been visiting there myself since I was little. It had tenants like the Pantry supermarket, Mujirushi Ryohin, Loft, and Futaba Books. Compared to the high-end department stores in Kyoto, it felt more like a community commercial facility for everyday use. It was only a five-minute walk from our apartment, and even as elementary schoolers, we were allowed to go there on our own.

Both of Naruse's parents are from Shiga Prefecture, and they seem to have a strong emotional connection to Seibu Otsu. Naruse's mother was born the very year Seibu Otsu opened, and she used to visit it all the time from her family home in Hikone. Apparently, the proximity to Seibu was a deciding factor when they bought their apartment.

On the other hand, my parents are from outside the prefecture. They don't share the unique passion Shiga residents have for Seibu, Heiwado, or Takanori Nishikawa. My mother, who was born in Yokohama, openly looks down on Shiga, saying things like, "If Seibu disappears, there'll be nothing left here." Apparently, Oh!Me Otsu Terrace next door doesn't count as a commercial facility to her.
"Starting in August, Gururin Wide will be doing live broadcasts from Seibu Otsu. I'm going to be on TV every day, so I want you to check it, Shimazaki."

Gururin Wide is a program broadcast from 5:55 PM to 6:45 PM on Biwa Tele, Shiga Prefecture's only local station. Even if she meant every day, the show is off on weekends and holidays, so it would only be about twenty times in total.
"Sure, but aren't you going to record it?"
"I shouldn't waste hard drive space on a scheme like this."
I thought this was exactly the kind of thing worth using hard drive space for, but I never could understand Naruse's standards.
"I might not be able to watch every single day, though."
"Just whenever you can. I'm counting on you."
Being the dutiful friend I am, as soon as I got home, I set a recording for Gururin Wide on Monday using the TV guide. Watching Naruse was my job.

Naruse always thinks big. In our elementary school graduation yearbook, she wrote that her dream for the future was to "live to be two hundred." I wondered if she planned to use cryogenics or body modification, but she said she intended to live to two hundred as a regular old lady.

I pointed out that the Guinness World Record was 122, so 200 might be a bit of a stretch. Naruse just looked at me with a straight face and said, "By then, everyone—including you, Shimazaki—will be dead, so there'll be no way to verify it." While I felt a bit sad that I wouldn't be able to witness the full history of Akari Naruse, I vowed to stay by her side and watch her for as long as I could.

Recently, she declared she would get a perfect score of 500 on her final exams. She ended up with 490, but even when she misses her goal, she never gets discouraged. Naruse says that if you say a hundred big things and even one of them comes true, people will think, "Wow, that person is incredible." That's why she thinks it's important to keep speaking your goals into existence. When I asked how that was different from just being a blowhard, she thought for a moment and admitted, "It's the same thing."
On August 3rd, the first day of the live broadcasts, I was already sitting on the sofa with the TV on five minutes before the show started, despite having set the recording.

I hadn't watched Gururin Wide properly since fifth grade. In other words, it wasn't the kind of show I'd normally be interested in. For the "Soap Bubble Prodigy" segment, the school must have cooperated, because the teacher had announced during the homeroom meeting, "Akari Naruse will be on Biwa Tele's Gururin Wide this evening." Even so, I figured I'd be the only one watching, so I was surprised by my classmates' reactions the next day.

At 5:55 PM, the show began with the Gururin Wide logo and some cheap-sounding BGM. After the sponsor credits, the live broadcast from Seibu Otsu started immediately. While shoppers went about their business naturally, Naruse was standing there solely to be on TV. With her shoulder-length black hair, white non-woven mask, and her black school skirt and white socks, she would have looked like an ordinary middle school girl. But for some reason, she was wearing a baseball jersey. Based on the "Lions" logo on the chest and where she was standing, it had to be a Seibu Lions jersey. I had never heard a single thing about Naruse being a baseball fan. In each hand, she gripped a plastic mini-bat, which appeared to be cheering gear.

The electronic signboard in front of the store read, "29 days until closing." While the reporter was saying, "We're doing the countdown to closing here," Naruse stood right there, staring straight into the camera. The reporter seemed to have labeled Naruse as someone strange and ignored her, instead pointing the microphone at a middle-aged woman who had just come out of the store carrying a blue and green patterned paper bag. The woman gave a comment that anyone could have said, yet perfectly met the TV station's expectations: "I've been here so many times, so I'm sad to see it go."
"That's all for our live report from Seibu Otsu," the reporter concluded, and the screen switched back to the studio.

I pulled up my tablet and did a proxy ego-search to see if anyone was mentioning Naruse on Twitter. I searched for likely keywords like "Gururin Wide," "Biwa Tele," "Seibu," and "Lions," but I couldn't find any tweets like that.

I kept watching Gururin Wide until the end of the program. It finished with a "Lady Luck" promoting the Summer Jumbo Lottery, an appeal from the Shiga Dental Association to "take care of your teeth," information about a new takeout bento shop in Nagahama, and some viewer emails. They never went back to Seibu Otsu.

After the show, Naruse stopped by my place. I thought maybe I should have recorded it for her, but since she'd specifically said not to waste hard drive space, I figured it would be bad manners for me to do so.
"Did you see me?"
"I saw you, you were definitely on screen. Was that a Lions jersey?"
"It was."

Naruse pulled the jersey out of her backpack to show me. The back had the number 1 and the name KURIYAMA. Apparently, Naruse had just bought it on a whim online and didn't even know who Kuriyama was. She figured since it was number 1, he must be a key player.
"It was pretty suspicious, but there's no doubt you stood out."
When I gave her my blunt opinion, she looked satisfied and said, "That's good to hear."

On August 4th, I watched Gururin Wide from the living room sofa again. My mother, who works as a receptionist at a nearby dentist's office, was off that day and watched with me. When Naruse appeared on screen, she burst out laughing and said, "She looks like a total suspicious character!"

My mother is another person who has watched Naruse grow up. She never says anything bad about Naruse to me, but there's always this underlying vibe of, "This kid is weird." Recently, she's started to find it amusing, saying things like, "Akari-chan is really a riot."
"Apparently, she's going to go every day until Seibu closes."
"That's great. You should go be on TV too, Miyuki."
My mother's suggestion was completely unexpected.
"But I don't have a jersey."
"Well, you don't necessarily need a jersey, do you?"
When I said I'd pass because it was embarrassing, she lent me a pair of sunglasses.

On August 5th, I headed to Seibu Otsu. Naruse was already there, jersey on and ready. When she saw me, she raised her right hand with the air of an old guy who's a die-hard baseball fan and said, "Yo." To maintain social distance, we stood about two meters apart, with the countdown display and the store map between us.

When I put on the sunglasses, Naruse said happily, "You look like Jun Miura," but I had no idea who Jun Miura was. My outfit was a plain T-shirt and denim pants; I made sure to stay just a supporting act for Naruse.

Seeing the behind-the-scenes of the live broadcast was a fresh experience. The female reporter I'd seen on TV had a high, clear voice, but at the filming site, her voice didn't carry as much as I expected. Every time the reporter moved, the cameraman moved in sync. The reporter pointed the microphone at a young mother pushing a stroller. An Akachan Honpo bag was hanging from the stroller. She was probably giving a comment like, "It'll be inconvenient once Seibu Otsu is gone."
As soon as the staff's light went out, Naruse quickly took off her jersey and tucked it into her backpack.
"I recorded it, so come over and watch."
I used the hard drive to check how I looked. I brought Naruse home and played back Gururin Wide.
"We're on screen more clearly than I thought."
Just as Naruse had said, we were frequently caught on camera standing near the countdown display.
"I wonder if people can tell it's me."
"Anyone who knows you would definitely recognize you."
Naruse looked so at home there that it seemed natural, whereas I, with most of my face hidden by sunglasses and a mask, looked far more suspicious.

When I searched on Twitter, I finally found a tweet saying, "I'm curious about that person in the jersey who's always in the live shots from Seibu Otsu." When I showed the tablet screen to Naruse, she nodded deeply and said knowingly, "If you're on screen three times, people start to think of you as a regular."

On August 6th and 7th, Naruse stood at the entrance of Seibu Otsu, finishing the first week of broadcasts. I could have gone if I'd wanted to, but the heat was just too much for me. It was much better to watch Gururin Wide in an air-conditioned room.
"Well, the first week ended smoothly, thanks to Shimazaki."

After the Friday broadcast, Naruse came to my house. Even though we lived in the same building, she didn't usually come over this often. I felt it was a bit of a hassle being made into her accomplice, but being relied on didn't feel too bad.
On Twitter, I saw a new tweet from someone named Takuro: "Lions Girl is on again today." It didn't mention Gururin Wide or Seibu Otsu, but given the timing, it was definitely about Naruse.

Furthermore, Naruse had apparently been approached at the site by a lady who told her, "You're always on TV, aren't you?" She was leaving an impression in the memories of at least three Shiga residents.
"Why did you decide to go every day?"
When I asked, Naruse adjusted the wire of her mask and answered.
"Making memories of this summer, I guess."

This year, due to COVID-19, school events had been cancelled or scaled back across the board. I was in the badminton club, but the summer tournaments were gone, and summer practice was only in the mornings. Plus, summer vacation had been shortened to about three weeks, from August 1st to August 23rd, making the summer itself feel thin. The closing of Seibu Otsu was the big event of our eighth-grade summer.
"Are you coming again, Shimazaki?"
I wanted to support Naruse in making her memories, but I really didn't want to go outside in this heat if I could help it.
"I'll go if I can."
When I said that, Naruse's face lit up.
"Then wear this when you do."
Naruse handed me a Seibu Lions jersey. It was number 3, with the name YAMAKAWA written above the number.
"You went out of your way to buy two?"
"Just in case something happens."
After a moment's hesitation, I accepted the jersey.
On August 11th, after the three-day weekend, I stood in front of Seibu Otsu wearing the YAMAKAWA jersey. I decided not to wear the sunglasses, fearing I might stand out even more than Naruse.
The program staff pretended not to notice us, but I could almost see a thought bubble above their heads saying, "There are more of them now."

The stance was likely set because the reporter had avoided Naruse on the first day. If they had been friendly from the start, they might have had some small talk like, "Oh, you brought a friend today?"

Then again, I couldn't rule out the possibility that Naruse was the one avoiding the staff. Deciding not to dig too deep, I stood in front of the main entrance, keeping my social distance from Naruse.
Today's interview subject was an elderly woman. The station must have preferred seniors who likely had deep sentimental ties to Seibu Otsu over kids like us.

After the broadcast, I watched the recording at my house. I hadn't noticed while I was standing there, but shoppers were walking around us to avoid us. Since that was a nuisance, I decided that from tomorrow, Naruse would stand next to the countdown display as usual, and I would move to a different spot.

Next, I checked Twitter and was disappointed to find that no one had mentioned Gururin Wide. I guess I had been hoping, deep down, that someone would find us. Naruse said confidently, "Most people who watch Gururin Wide are old ladies, after all."
"By the way, do you think we could write something on our masks? Like an ad or a message."
Naruse took out a ruler, held it up to the mask she was wearing, and asked me to read the measurements. It was about twelve centimeters high and eighteen centimeters wide.
"Hmm, you probably can't write much on there, can you?"
I suggested holding a fan like the ones Johnny's fans use, but Naruse countered that we shouldn't rely on props.
"The important thing is to make effective use of the masks. Since we'll be living with masks for a while, there's no reason not to take advantage of them."

On August 12th, Naruse had written "Thank you Seibu Otsu Store" in black marker across two lines on her mask. The letters "Sei" and "Store" were mostly hidden because the mask was distorted to fit her face, but you could guess the meaning from the context.

As we'd discussed the day before, we changed our positions and maintained social distance. When a boy who looked like he was in early elementary school pointed at Naruse and shouted, "Look, it says thank you!", the person who seemed to be his mother took his hand and hurried into the store.
Back home, I checked the recording. I could see that there was something written on Naruse's mask, but I couldn't make out the actual words.
"Isn't two characters the limit for this size? Or maybe a logo."

When I said that, Naruse nodded and said, "A McDonald's, Nike, or Apple ad would work." I doubted such global companies would advertise on Naruse's mask, but I got the message that she was aiming for the world stage.

On August 13th, Naruse wrote "Gratitude" on her mask. When I checked the recording later, there was a moment where she was caught in a larger shot at the edge of the screen, and I could read the word "Gratitude."
"Looks like you can fit two characters."

However, there's only so much you can convey with two characters. "Gratitude" wasn't bad, but when Naruse wore it, it had a suspicious vibe, like some new religion. The plan for effective mask usage was put on hold for the time being.

When I checked Twitter, I saw that Takuro, who had mentioned Naruse before, had posted, "There are two Lions Girls now!" A warm, tingly feeling, somewhere between happiness and embarrassment, welled up in my chest.

"Only a few people actually write things online. Even if Gururin Wide's ratings are incredibly low, if just 0.1% of Shiga Prefecture's 1.4 million residents are watching, that's 1,400 people. A few of them must have noticed us."

I hadn't really thought about it at the filming site, but there were viewers on the other side of the TV. Thinking about us in our Lions jerseys appearing in their eyes gave me an indescribable sense of excitement.
On August 14th, I met up with Naruse on the way, but when we reached Seibu Otsu five minutes before the show started, the usual filming crew wasn't there.
"Oh, did they stop the live broadcasts?"
Despite the high temperature, I felt my hands and feet go cold. Ignoring my agitation, Naruse silently studied the store map.
"It's probably the top floor."

I went to the seventh floor with Naruse in the elevator. As we stepped out of the restaurant area, we saw the "Seibu Otsu 44-Year History Exhibition" panel display and the filming crew. I could tell that the staff member holding the microphone saw us and looked away. Naruse put on her jersey, nonchalantly moved to a position where she'd likely be on camera, and turned to face the photo panels on the wall.

I put on my jersey and looked at the photos too. The panels, which looked like enlarged faded photographs, conveyed what Seibu Otsu was like when it first opened. A spacious food department, an elegant cafe, the now-defunct multi-purpose hall on the sixth floor, the giant Biwako-shaped atrium connecting the sixth and seventh floors, and "Bird Paradise" where birds flew around. Everywhere was bustling with people. The Seibu Otsu I knew was always deserted. People say it was because customers were taken by Aeon Mall Kusatsu, or because of the rise of online shopping. The people in the photos all looked so happy. I wondered if I would ever make a face like that in a commercial facility in the future.
While I was absorbed in the photos, the broadcast ended. Naruse had already taken off her jersey.
"I'm going to stay and look a bit more."
When I said that, Naruse just said "I see" and headed home alone. I thought she was a cold-hearted person, but this kind of behavior was nothing new.

The Seibu Otsu 44-Year History Exhibition spanned the entire wall of the seventh floor. I had started by looking at the photo zone from the store's opening, and the photos were arranged chronologically from there.
2006, the year I was born, was the store's 30th anniversary milestone. The interior looked almost identical to the scenery I knew, but the customers' fashion felt a little old.
"Hey there, you're the girl who's always on TV, aren't you?"

Suddenly approached by a lady I didn't know, I realized I'd forgotten to take off my jersey. I reflexively answered "Ah, yes," but the one who's always on TV is Naruse. I wanted to say it was a case of mistaken identity, but people don't exactly come shopping in Seibu jerseys every day, so it was no wonder she got us mixed up.
"Good, I was hoping I could give this to you if we met."
The lady, who was wearing a lace mask like Yuriko Koike, pulled out a blue baseball cap. It had the face of a white lion looking to the side and the "Lions" logo.
"Here, you can have this. It's a bit old, but I've washed it properly."
I tried to politely decline, but the lady said, "Don't be shy," and practically forced it on me before leaving.
Thinking things had gotten complicated, I stopped by Naruse's house.
When I rang the intercom, Naruse's mother came out. She looked a bit down, though I felt she might have always been like that.
"Oh, Miyuki-chan. Thanks for always hanging out with her."

My image of Naruse's mother was someone who was always quiet and smiling. She didn't seem like a "tiger mom" type. Naruse's current personality is probably the result of her mother smilingly accepting everything she wanted to do.
"Um, you're originally from Shiga, aren't you?"
"Yes, I am."

She looked surprised that I'd spoken to her. I didn't have much memory of talking to Naruse's mother myself. Even now, I felt there was a wall between us that made it hard to call her "Auntie," so I opted for "Akari-chan's mom."
"For someone who's been coming here for years, what does the closing of Seibu feel like?"
"Well, it's sad, of course, but there's nothing we can do about it now. I guess we just wait for the day."
Naruse's mother said this with a smile still on her face. Naruse must have noticed I was there, as she came from the back of the house.
"What's up?"
"I have something to give you."
I'd intended to just talk at the door, but Naruse's mother invited me inside.
"After that, a lady I didn't know spoke to me and gave me this."
I showed Naruse the baseball cap I'd received.
"She said to give it to the girl who's always on TV. She said it's used but it's been washed."
When I told her the story with a little embellishment, Naruse put on the cap without a second thought.
"I'll wear this from Monday."
Honestly, I'd been relieved because I didn't want to wear it myself.
"Since we don't know where they'll show up next, it's probably better to get there early."
I'd gone blank when the filming crew wasn't in front of the main entrance. I don't know why I got so worked up. Naruse had been much calmer.
"Well, I don't know if I'll be going or not, though."
We were starting to seem like a unit by default, but I maintained my stance of "I'll go if I can." This project belonged to Naruse.
On Monday, August 17th, after the Obon holidays, my club activities resumed. It was an easy schedule from 9:00 AM to 11:30 AM.
"Miyuki, weren't you on TV the other day?"
Haruka, who's in the same club, spoke to me.
"Yeah. I'm keeping Naruse company."
Haruka laughed and said, "That sounds tough."
"I saw you too. It was Friday, right? The Seibu photo exhibition thing."
Mizune joined the conversation.
"Wait, I saw you in front of the entrance. You were wearing a baseball jersey, weren't you?"

Oh right, why hadn't I realized this sooner? Even if they don't watch it regularly, they might happen to tune in to Gururin Wide by chance. Even if the two of them only saw a glimpse, if they put the pieces together like a puzzle, what I was doing would be exposed.
"I go almost every day. With Naruse."
I tried to shift the blame to Naruse, but wearing the jersey and accompanying her was my own choice. I expected them to be creeped out, but Haruka and Mizune just burst out laughing.
"I had no idea they were broadcasting every day! I want to try going too."
"Me too."

I should have been happy to have more company, but I wasn't feeling it. I was in "Naruse mode," which was different from my "club activities mode." Still, I couldn't exactly turn them down, so I told them that the show starts at 5:55 PM and while it's usually at the main entrance, we wouldn't know the exact location until the day.

I'd planned to slack off this week, but now that Haruka and Mizune were going, I had no choice but to go too. Arriving a bit early, I was relieved to see the filming crew at the main entrance. Naruse was wearing the Lions cap as promised. I hoped the lady who gave it to her was watching on TV.
"Someone else I don't know gave me this just now."
Naruse showed me a blue wristband on her left wrist.
"You look like a huge Lions fan now."
"There's no doubt that I am a Seibu fan."
With that, she took her stance with her mini-bats.
"Some girls from the badminton club might come today. I told them we come every day, and they said they wanted to check it out."
Naruse just said "I see," appearing uninterested.
Haruka and Mizune came out of the store just before the live broadcast started. Naruse was already focused on the camera.
"So this is where they do it."
When the two of them stopped near me, I urged them to maintain social distance. If things got too crowded here, there was a chance they'd cancel the broadcasts from tomorrow onwards.

As Haruka and Mizune took up positions a little way off, the reporter pointed the microphone at them. I couldn't hide my surprise. They chose to talk to a pair of middle school girls in regular clothes instead of Naruse, who was broadcasting Seibu love from every pore. Haruka and Mizune answered the questions with smiles. It felt as if a thick sheet of acrylic had suddenly appeared between me and the two of them.

After the broadcast, we packed up to head home. Haruka and Mizune excitedly reported, "They talked to us!" I felt a surge of jealousy rising from the pit of my stomach. "That's nice," I said curtly, and headed home with Naruse.
"Naruse is the one who should've been interviewed."
When I voiced my true feelings, Naruse laughed.
"Not at all. The station just wanted comments from girls like that."
She didn't sound like she was putting on a brave face; she seemed to truly accept it. Her composure was infuriating.
"Since you're here anyway, don't you want to be interviewed? Or be on screen more?"
Naruse replied with an immediate "No." She looked like she couldn't understand why I was getting so worked up. I left her behind and hurried home.

On August 18th, after a night's sleep, my mood had shifted, and I was able to interact with Haruka and Mizune as usual. After we talked about yesterday's events, saying things like "I never expected to be spoken to," I asked in as light a tone as possible, "Are you going again?" They just laughed and said, "I think we're good."

Influenced by their "we're good," I decided not to go to Seibu that day. Part of me also didn't really want to see Naruse. The broadcast was from the main entrance, and Naruse was standing next to the countdown display which read "14." Naturally, the microphone wasn't pointed her way.
I wasn't going every day like Naruse, nor was I being interviewed like Haruka and Mizune. When I thought about whether there was any point in me going, I just got fed up with it all.
On August 21st, Naruse stopped by after the broadcast.
"How was it?"
When Naruse asked, I remembered her original request for me to "watch the TV." Even if I didn't go, Naruse surely wouldn't have minded.
"I saw you, you were on screen."
As usual, I'd been watching every day. Even when I thought I didn't need to watch, as soon as it hit 5:50 PM, I'd realize it was almost time for Gururin Wide.
The broadcast was from the sixth floor, showing the final bargain sale at Loft. Naruse was caught clearly on camera, drawing glances from other customers.
"Maybe they broadcast from inside the store on Fridays."
If that pattern held, there was a good chance next Friday would be from inside as well.
"School starts next week; what are you going to do on club days?"
"I'll get permission to leave early so I can make it in time. I'll take all my gear and go straight from school."
Naruse would probably manage to carry it out until the final day without anyone scolding her.
"That sounds tough."
I felt like it was completely someone else's problem now. Club activities lasted until 6:00 PM, and I had no intention of leaving early just for the broadcast.
"I won't be able to watch it live anymore, either."
"That's fine. Thanks for keeping me company until now."
Naruse left after saying that. Even though I'd been the one to quit, I felt like I'd been dropped by Naruse.

On Sunday afternoon, while channel-surfing, I came across a game between Seibu and Orix. For some reason, I felt like watching and put down the remote. When my dad teased me, asking, "Are you watching baseball now, Miyuki?", I just gave a vague "Just for today."

The Seibu players weren't wearing the white jerseys Naruse and I had; they were in navy ones. In the top of the sixth, Kuriyama, wearing number 1, came to the plate. I saw Naruse's image from Gururin Wide overlapping with Kuriyama. He connected on the first pitch, and the ball sailed into the stands. Even though I didn't know much about baseball rules, I knew this was a home run. Kuriyama had a sharp, handsome face, and he reminded me of Sugimoto-kun from the soccer club.

August 24th was the opening ceremony for the second semester, and club activities were off. Other than Kawasaki-kun in the seat next to mine pointing out, "You were on TV in a Seibu jersey," nothing noteworthy happened.
"Did anyone in your class say anything about you being on TV, Naruse?"
"No. Only a few people would say it to my face, but I'm sure some noticed."
It was true; I wouldn't go out of my way to tell a classmate I rarely spoke to that I'd seen them on TV.
"Can I come too today?"
Since I'd be getting home late due to club activities starting tomorrow, this was my last chance. Even though I didn't really need permission, I asked, and Naruse replied, "Of course."

Realizing I'd forgotten to do a proxy ego-search, I went home and searched Twitter. Takuro, who was the first to call us "Lions Girls," had mentioned us several times since then. There was also a tweet from a housewife in Kusatsu: "The girl in the Seibu jersey shows up every time I watch Gururin Wide. Does she go every day? lol"
When I reached the main entrance of Seibu Otsu ten minutes before the show, Naruse was staring at the countdown display, which now read "8 days left," with a troubled expression.
"If this keeps up, the final day will be '1 day left.' But shouldn't it properly be '0 days left'?"

Now that she mentioned it, she was right. But there was no way they'd make such a blatant mistake. While we were discussing how they couldn't just suddenly subtract two days tomorrow even if it was an error, a girl about five years old approached us.
"Look, the baseball ladies! There's two of them today!"

The girl handed me a piece of paper. Looking at it, I saw two people drawn in the same clothes. One was wearing a blue hat, and the other wasn't. The person who seemed to be her mother said, "We always watch you on TV." I reflexively replied, "Thank you very much," and the girl waved as she and her mother went into the store, saying "Bye-bye!" I was thinking it was strange for them to be at Seibu at this time if they always watched the show, when I glanced at Naruse and was startled to see her eyes welling up.
"I can't believe this is happening."

I handed the fan art to Naruse. She tucked it carefully into her backpack and turned to face the front with her mini-bats. Today, the reporter was interviewing a pair of women who appeared to be a mother and daughter at the final bargain sale.

When the broadcast ended and I took off the jersey, it felt like summer was over. I wondered if high school baseball players felt like this too. They'd probably be mad if I compared us to them, though.
"I'll wash this and give it back to you."
"No, you should keep it for a while, Shimazaki."
Thinking she might ask me for something else, I tucked the jersey into my bag.
On August 25th, I checked the recording after getting home from club activities.

Naruse was holding a stuffed mascot of the Seibu Lions, which someone must have given her. While the plan for mask advertising had fallen through, I felt she was somewhat playing a role in PR for the Seibu Lions. In fact, it was because of Naruse that I'd learned who Kuriyama was.
On August 26th, she was on screen in her usual spot again. My mother commented, "She's starting to blend into the scenery now."

When the project first started, I thought some copycats might appear. Maybe no one was that bored, or maybe people didn't find the ratings of Gururin Wide appealing, but no one ever tried to claim that prime spot next to the countdown display.
Naruse visited me after 7:00 PM.
"I made it into the newspaper."
Naruse showed me a copy of the local "Oumi Nippo." It was a series about the closing of Seibu Otsu, featuring local residents.
Naruse was one of several people featured. There was a photo too, but her face was mostly hidden by her baseball cap and mask.

"Akari Naruse (14), a local eighth-grader, has been visiting Seibu Otsu in a Seibu Lions jersey. 'This summer, there was nothing to do because of COVID, so I came up with the idea of visiting Seibu Otsu, which has done so much for me. My goal is to keep going until the final day,' she said."
It was funny to think that the "Akari Naruse (14)" in the article was the same person standing right in front of me.
"Three more times."
Even though it was only a five-minute walk from home, it must have been tough going there at the same time every day in the heat. There were only three weekdays left.
"I hope I can make it to the end."
Naruse said something uncharacteristically weak, but I didn't think much of it at the time.

On August 27th, even though it was a Thursday, the broadcast was from inside the store, showcasing the message board near the general information desk. Three boards, each about two meters square, were set up around the clock tower, and they were all being filled up with visitors' message cards.
The broadcast caught Naruse in the act of writing a message. I was curious about what she was writing, but finding her card among all those would be like looking for a needle in a haystack.

On August 28th, the broadcast was from inside as the pattern predicted, this time from the "Hagumama Center" on the fifth floor. It's a play area for children with slides, play kitchens, and picture books, but it had apparently been off-limits since spring due to COVID. Behind a woman with a child commenting that "this is the place where my child took their first steps," Naruse stood blended into the toy department.

At the end of the segment, the reporter announced, "Our next broadcast will be on August 31st, the final day of business for Seibu Otsu. Since it's the last day, Gururin Wide will be reporting entirely from Seibu Otsu!" Gururin Wide ends at 6:45 PM. I could make it by 6:30 PM even after club activities. With this unexpected last chance appearing, I felt a strong urge to go. I was glad I hadn't returned the jersey. I decided to tell Naruse on the way to school on Monday that I'd be at the final broadcast.

On August 30th, I went to Seibu Otsu with my mother. The shelves for the final bargain sale were already mostly empty, and there were long lines at the registers. It was the first time I'd seen Seibu Otsu so crowded. My mother made one of those typical closing-day comments: "If it had been this busy all the time, it wouldn't have gone out of business."

I hadn't been able to tell from the broadcast, but the message board at the entrance had an outline of Lake Biwa. The rule was to stick blue cards on the lake part and orange cards on the land part. I took a quick look, but I couldn't find Naruse's card. Reading messages like "I'm so glad Seibu was in Otsu," "Our first date was here," "Thanks for all the memories," and "This was my favorite place" made me feel all emotional. I wanted to leave a message too, so I wrote, "I've been coming here since I was little. Thank you for everything," and stuck it on.
On the morning of August 31st, when I left the house at the usual time, Naruse was in the apartment entrance in her regular clothes.
"I'm staying home from school today."

For a second, I thought she was taking the day off to prepare for Gururin Wide. I was about to say something like, "Wow, you're really going all out for the final day," when Naruse, looking uncharacteristically solemn, said, "My grandmother died."
"Your grandmother? The one in Hikone?"
"Yeah. My family and I are heading over there now."
"What about Gururin Wide?"
I knew it might be inappropriate, but I couldn't help asking. Naruse silently shook her head. She looked like she was telling me not to ask such a thing.
"I just wanted to let you know, Shimazaki. See ya."
Naruse left after saying that, disappearing toward the elevator.

I went to school as usual, but my mind was elsewhere the entire time. During classes, all I could think about was Naruse and Gururin Wide. I felt conflicted; part of me knew there was nothing to be done under the circumstances, yet another part of me wondered if there was some way things could have worked out. As someone entrusted with the "just in case," I decided that I should at least be there from the start of the program, so I left club activities early and headed home.
While preparing for the final broadcast at home, I searched for "Seibu Otsu" on Twitter and found it overflowing with voices of people mourning the closure. Apparently, it was packed again today.

When I changed the search term to "Gururin Wide," the number of posts dropped significantly. Takuro, who had been following Naruse from early on, had tweeted on Friday, "Guess it's almost time for the last look at Lions Girls..." I wanted to tell him that Naruse couldn't make it due to a family tragedy, but I'd been taught not to reveal personal information that wasn't my own. I thought about writing "Naruse is absent" on my mask, but unless they were a die-hard viewer, they probably wouldn't know the difference between me and Naruse anyway.
Still, I felt like writing something on my mask since it was the last day, so I wrote "Thank You" in large letters.

When I arrived at the main entrance ten minutes before the show started, I realized I'd made a mistake. There was already a huge crowd of onlookers. People who had come out for the final day were likely stopping when they saw the TV cameras.
The countdown display was surrounded by people taking commemorative photos. Everyone was using their smartphones to capture the "1 day left" sign.
When I put on my jersey to get ready, I felt the eyes of the crowd on me.
"Thanks for your hard work this past month."

A woman around forty years old approached me and gave me a Seibu Lions towel. She then asked, "Can I take a photo with you?", and for some reason, we ended up taking a two-shot. Just as I was thinking it was fine if it made her happy, I heard a voice say, "That one's a fake." Looking over, I saw a white-haired man glaring at me with a severe expression.
"That's not the girl who's always on screen."

I couldn't believe there was such a devoted viewer here. Compared to Naruse, who had a perfect attendance record, I hadn't put in enough days. My commitment to being just a supporting act had backfired.
"I'm her friend."
"Liar! You can't fool me like that! You're not even wearing a hat!"

The woman who gave me the towel stood there, looking lost. I had nothing to prove I was Naruse's friend. Even if I told him about Naruse's grandmother passing away, he probably wouldn't believe me. People around us were looking on with "I don't want to get involved" expressions. On top of that, Gururin Wide was about to start any second.
"Shimazaki!"
Looking toward the source of the voice, I saw the real Akari Naruse, wearing her number 1 jersey, crossing the pedestrian walk. She had her hat and wristband on, too.
"I made it," Naruse said as she ran up to me. She had "Thank You" written on her mask as well.
"Did something happen?"
I was so relieved I almost cried. The man who had been bothering me had vanished into thin air. The woman who gave me the towel also looked relieved.
"I'll explain later."
I draped the blue towel around Naruse's neck.

The broadcast began, and the reporter started pointing the microphone at people in the crowd. Usually, they only talked to one group, but today they spoke to a second, then a third. I was hoping they might turn to Naruse, but the interviews ended with the fourth group. The filming crew began to move off in a cluster.
"Just now, a random guy hassled me, calling me a fake."
"That's rough. Sorry I'm late."
I never expected an apology from Naruse.
"It's okay. I'm just glad you're here. Is everything all right with your grandmother?"
"The wake is tomorrow. My relatives all said Grandma would be happier if I came here today, too."
I felt a surge of gratitude toward the relatives who had sent Naruse on her way.

The filming crew moved up through Seibu Otsu as if looking back on its history, going from the food department on the first floor to women's wear on the second, and men's wear on the fourth. Only Naruse, myself, and a group of elementary schoolers followed them. When one of the kids asked, "Why are you wearing baseball jerseys?", Naruse replied, "This is my uniform."

The final segment of the program was from the sixth-floor terrace. The store manager stood with Seibu Otsu at his back, talking to the reporter for the camera. We, the onlookers, stood behind the manager, spaced out to avoid crowding.
"I'm glad it's summer," Naruse said.
"Why's that?"
"Because if it were dark and cold, it would feel even lonelier right now."
And so, Naruse dedicated the summer of her eighth-grade year to the Seibu Otsu department store.
On September 3rd, after Naruse returned from her bereavement leave, we went to see Seibu Otsu after club activities.

The empty Seibu Otsu seemed to have aged rapidly. It was hard to believe it was the same building from three days ago; the wear and tear was so much more noticeable. The SEIBU logo at the entrance had been stripped away, and the signs were covered with sheets. While employees seemed to be going in and out to pack things up, demolition work would likely begin soon.

Naruse's grandmother, who had been hospitalized with an illness, had apparently looked forward to watching Gururin Wide every day. She'd been happy right up until the August 28th broadcast, saying things like, "Akari's on again today." However, her condition had suddenly worsened late on the night of the 30th, and she passed away on the morning of August 31st. The countdown to the store's closing, Naruse's regular spot, had turned out to be the countdown of her grandmother's life.
"Were you going to Seibu for your grandmother's sake, Naruse?"
"I was somewhat aware of that, but it wasn't the main reason. I just wanted to take on a challenge that I could actually do during a time like this."
Personally, I'd wanted to see Naruse go viral more, but it never really blew up to that extent. I felt I'd reached the limits of Biwa Tele and Gururin Wide.

Still, at least a few people will remember Naruse as part of their memories of Seibu Otsu's closing. The people who gave her Seibu gear, the child who drew her a picture, the Twitter accounts that tweeted about her, the newspaper reporter who interviewed her, the viewers of Gururin Wide—they are all precious witnesses to the history of Akari Naruse.
"One day, I'm going to build a department store in Otsu."
"Good luck with that."
Hoping Naruse's words would come true, I looked up at the building that used to be Seibu Otsu.
